chapter: New York 1936-39 (second pass of the transcript)
title: Skeets Talbot at the Black Cat and Hammond's jam nights (second pass)
summary: Repeat of the Village club's white clientele and John Hammond's concert-style jamming.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Now, after you left Billy Hicks, you were with him for a couple of years.
Then I went with Skeets Talbot.
Yeah, I don't know too much about that band either.
Well, Skeets Talbot, he had a band down in the village called the Black Cat.
Oh, I've heard of the Black Cat.
And we were there a couple of years.
How big was that band?
Six.
Six pieces.
Oh, and let me add, this place was a converted garage but the entertainment was black but the clientele was white. We didn't have any black clientele.
Well, they even did that in Harlem.
Amanda Randolph --
Well, I remember hearing about the
Black Cat and reading about it, that Kenny Clark played down there, that was afterwards.
No, no. Freddie Green --
Yeah, that's where Basie heard Freddie Green.
That's where John Hammond heard Freddie Green --
Right, right.
But John Hammond lived in the area on Sullivan Street and he used to bring his family to dinner.
Yeah.

We worked seven days a week from seven until four, seven days a week. Then, what I wanted to say was that John was the one that introduced listening, a listening audience, concert wise. Prior to this, he would come in and we had a small dance floor and he had the ways of pushing the chairs out on the floor where you could sit and he would bring Benny Goodman, Harry James, the Count, Mary Lou Williams, Teddy Wilson --
To listen?
No, to play.
To play?
To jam.
Oh, I see.
So that nobody would dance, and I still
say that this is the beginning of concert-wise jamming.
